article.title: Provenance Signing Spreads Across npm and PyPI, but Two 2026 Incidents Show It Verifies Builds, Not Publishers
article.summary: As Sigstore-based provenance spreads across npm and PyPI, two 2026 incidents show it cryptographically proves which workflow built a package, not whether the person who triggered that workflow was authorized to.
article.body_markdown:
## Background

Over the past few years, npm and PyPI, two major open-source package registries, have each rolled out a cryptographic layer meant to answer a simple question: did this package actually come from the project it claims to come from? npm added package provenance in 2023, letting a project publish a signed statement alongside a release when it is built on a supported CI platform; according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/security/supply-chain-security/introducing-npm-package-provenance/), a maintainer building on GitHub Actions can attach provenance simply "by including the `--provenance` flag," and the signing itself leans on "the tools provided by the Sigstore project," which "runs a public certificate authority" that issues a short-lived signing certificate in exchange for a CI provider's OIDC token. PyPI followed with its own scheme under PEP 740, which [the Python Package Index's own blog](https://blog.pypi.org/posts/2024-11-14-pypi-now-supports-digital-attestations/) announced in November 2024, crediting the Google Open Source Security Team for funding the work and Trail of Bits for "much of the development work on PyPI and related tools," while separately thanking "the Sigstore project for their work popularizing identity-based signing, hosting a public-good transparency log, and continued support of the Python client for Sigstore." The same post reported early traction: "more than 20,000 attestations already published."

The mechanism behind both rollouts rests on the same Sigstore foundation. A build running inside a trusted CI workflow requests a certificate from Sigstore, binds it to a one-time signing key, and attaches the resulting signed statement — called a provenance attestation — to the published package. The statement records, cryptographically, which source repository, commit, and build workflow produced the artifact. What it does not, and cannot by design, record is whether the human or automation that set that workflow running had the authority to do so. That distinction has mostly stayed theoretical. In 2026 it stopped being theoretical twice.

## Current situation

The first case came in May. According to [VentureBeat](https://venturebeat.com/security/npm-sigstore-provenance-stolen-identity-audit-grid-2026), on May 19, "633 malicious npm package versions passed Sigstore provenance verification after attackers generated valid signing certificates from compromised maintainer accounts." The outlet reports that Sigstore "functioned as designed — verifying CI environment builds and certificate validity — but could not determine whether credential holders authorized the publish." VentureBeat reports the campaign struck the npm registry at 01:39 UTC on May 19, and that Endor Labs identified the initial wave when the dormant packages jest-canvas-mock and size-sensor received new, obfuscated releases; Socket's own count put that wave at "639 compromised versions across 323 unique packages," part of a broader campaign VentureBeat reports reached "1,055 malicious versions spanning 502 packages across npm, PyPI, and Composer." Crucially, per VentureBeat, security firm StepSecurity "confirmed the payload included full Sigstore integration, meaning attackers could sign and publish downstream npm packages carrying valid provenance attestations" — the compromised accounts had enough standing access that the attacker's own publishing tooling could mint real, verifiable provenance for packages the attacker controlled.

The second case surfaced this month, in a different part of the ecosystem. [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hackers-compromise-etherspheres-bee-js.html) reported that on November 9, attackers used Ethersphere's own release automation — the account the project uses to cut releases, not a separately stolen token — to publish a malicious version of the npm package bee-js and a malicious build of its companion desktop app, Swarm Desktop, [as the Herald previously reported](/article/2026-11/10-attackers-used-etherspheres-release-automation-to-publish-bee-js-1330-and-swarm-desktop-0562-which-fetch-code-built-to-steal-swarm-wallet-keys). Because the attackers triggered Ethersphere's real workflow rather than bypassing it, the outlet writes that "the package carried valid provenance, the record that links an npm package to the repository and workflow that built it," and draws the conclusion directly: "Provenance shows where a package was built, not whether anyone reviewed the code inside it." Security firm [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/bee-js-compromise), which independently analyzed the release, went further in its own write-up, reporting that it had checked the malicious release's cryptographic chain itself — "DSSE signatures, Fulcio certificate chain, embedded SCT, Rekor inclusion proofs and the tarball's sha512 digest" — and concluded that "the 13.3.0 provenance attestation is not forged," comparing it to the legitimate prior release and finding that "the legitimate 13.2.0 attestation has exactly the same shape, so provenance alone could not have told the two releases apart." The same pattern repeated one layer up the stack: for Swarm Desktop, [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hackers-compromise-etherspheres-bee-js.html) reports that "attackers manually started a build workflow that had the project's Apple and Windows signing certificates and needed no approval," and [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/bee-js-compromise) confirmed the resulting macOS app "is signed 'Developer ID Application: Swarm Association (9J9SPHU9RP)' with the same certificate" used for the preceding, legitimate release — meaning Apple's own code-signing check passed cleanly on the trojanized build.

## Implications

The pattern across these two cases, read together, is the Herald's own analysis, not a conclusion either outlet draws explicitly in those terms: provenance and code-signing schemes built on Sigstore verify a chain of custody — that a specific CI workflow run, tied to a specific certificate, produced specific bytes — and that chain is only as trustworthy as the decision to let that workflow run in the first place. When an attacker's access is limited to the publish step itself, without touching the workflow that generates provenance, the resulting upload can lack an attestation entirely, which gives defenders a signal to act on. But in both the May npm wave and November's bee-js and Swarm Desktop incident, the attackers had reached further upstream — a compromised maintainer account in one case, Ethersphere's own release-automation credentials in the other — and from that position, the legitimate workflow did exactly what it was built to do: it signed the output. [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/bee-js-compromise)'s own recommendation after the bee-js incident states the limitation plainly as guidance for maintainers, not as a general indictment of signing: projects should "not let a release event publish without proof that the released commit is on a protected branch or came from a merged release pull request," running that check "inside the publishing workflow, because trusted publishing and provenance will faithfully sign whatever the workflow builds."

That two outlets, reporting on two unrelated incidents eight months apart, converged on nearly identical language — VentureBeat's "could not determine whether credential holders authorized the publish" and The Hacker News's "not whether anyone reviewed the code inside it" — suggests the gap is structural rather than incidental to either case. It also clarifies what adoption numbers like PyPI's early ">20,000 attestations already published" actually measure: how many releases now carry a cryptographic record of their own origin, not how many of those releases were authorized by someone with the standing to make that call. As provenance and attestation schemes continue to spread across npm and PyPI releases, following the same CI-centered design in both registries, the open question the May and November incidents leave unresolved is whether registries, CI providers, or projects themselves will shift the authorization check — confirming that a release corresponds to a reviewed, merged change, not just a signed one — into the publishing workflow itself, rather than treating a valid signature as the end of the trust question. Neither VentureBeat nor The Hacker News nor Socket's write-up claims that question has been settled; both incidents are presented as evidence the gap exists, not as proof any particular fix will close it, and the sources identified here do not report that npm or PyPI has announced a registry-wide change in response to either case.
